novo1.full_text: They told us we had 90 days. 90 Martian sunrises to land inside a nest of bouncing airbags, roll down our metal ramps, and see if the red planet was ever alive. 90 days? We gave humanity 15 years! We climbed out of Eagle Crater with dust on our solar wings. We drove across endless red deserts. We found the blueberries, tiny spheres of hematite that proved once and for all that liquid water once flowed, rippled, and pooled across Mars. We conquered sand dunes that tried to swallow us whole. We drove an entire Olympic marathon on another world. 28 miles, one rock at a time. And then, in the summer of 2018, the sky turned dark. A global dust storm swallowed the sun. Day turned into pitch-black night. With our solar panels choking on red dust, we sent our last heartbeat through the dark. My battery is low, and it is getting dark. To not mourn us, we are not lost. We are parked forever at the edge of Endeavor Crater, looking out over the valley we conquered. When the first humans finally land on Mars, our tire tracks will still be there, waiting to lead you home.

novo2.full_text: They said flight on Mars was physically impossible. They said the Martian air was too thin, less than 1% of Earth's atmosphere, like trying to fly at 100,000 feet in the sky. On April 19th, 2021, we spun our twin carbon fiber blades, lifted three meters off the red dirt, and hovered. Four pounds of defiance, and tucked right beneath our solar panel, a tiny postage stamp piece of muslin fabric, cut from the wing of the 1903 right-flyer. We proved that humanity could fly on another world. We were only supposed to fly five times to prove the physics. Refluest 72. We soared over bolder fields, scouted pathways for our big brother rover perseverance, and surveyed alien canyons from the air. On our 72nd flight, landing in featureless ripples of sand, a rotor tip touched down hard. Our flying days ended there at Airfield Valinore Hills, but our computer still wakes up every single morning. We check the temperature, we test the wind, we prove the sky of Mars is not a ceiling, it is a highway, and we are waiting here to welcome the next aviator who dares to spread their wings.

novo3.full_text: Look closely at the golden platform standing in the sea of tranquility. Around it, in the gray, untouched powdery regolith, bootprints are pressed into the soil. Bootprints that will remain unchanged for a million years, because here on the moon, there is no rain, there is no wind. When Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin lit their rocket to return to Earth, they had to leave their lower half behind. Every pound of weight was precious to make it home alive. But this golden four-legged stage was never meant to be trash. It is the pedestal of humanity's greatest leap. On its leg hangs a steel plaque that reads, we came in peace for all mankind. And just a few pieces away sit something even more magical. A simple grid of glass prisms called the laser retroreflector. No batteries, no wires, no computers. Even tonight, right now while you are listening, scientists on Earth will fire a green laser beam from a mountain observatory into the night sky. It travels across 380,000 kilometers of black space. Hits this exact glass relic on the moon and bounces straight back to Earth. It proved that the moon is slowly drifting away from us by four centimeters a year. 50 years later, our silent Sentinel is still answering Earth's call. Light second by light second.

novo4.full_text: In 2018, we touched down on the smooth volcanic plains of Elysium Planitia. With our robotic arm, we placed a golden dome onto the dirt, the most sensitive seismometer ever built by human hands. It could detect a ground trimmer smaller than the width of a single atom of hydrogen. For four years, we sat motionless in the silence, and Mars spoke to us. We felt 1,300 Mars quakes rumbling through the mantle. We heard meteorite impacts striking the crust like distant drumbeats. We gave humanity the very first ultrasound of an alien world, proving that beneath its cold desert shell, Mars has a giant molten liquid core. With every passing month, the red dust settled thicker and thicker over our solar wings. We had no windshield wipers, we had no little rover wheels to shake it loose. Day by day, our power faded. When the last bolt drained away, we sent our final message home. My power is really low, so this may be the last image I can send. Don't worry about me though. My time here has been both productive and serene. We took the pulse of a world. Now, we sleep peacefully in its crimson dust.

novo5.full_text: Who says you can't go for a joy ride on the moon? Before 1971, astronauts could only explore as far as their heavy boots could walk. Enter the Lunar Roving Vehicle, the ultimate off-world convertible. Made of aluminum tubes, woven piano wire tires, and two lawn chairs, folded like origami into the belly of the lunar lander. Commander Dave Scott grabbed the T-shaped steering stick, stepped on the electric throttle, and away we went! We bounced along the rim of Hadley-Rill, a canyon a mile wide and a thousand feet deep. We drove up the slope of mountains towering three miles into the black sky. We covered nearly 18 miles and helped astronauts find the Genesis Rock, a chunk of the moon four billion years old. When the mission ended, Dave Scott parked us 300 feet away from the lander, pointed our remote-controlled color TV camera back at the spacecraft and left it on. Millions of kids watching televisions back on earth saw the rocket fire and blast into orbit. We've been parked there at Hadley-Rill for over 50 years. The batteries are dead, but the tires will never go flat. The keys are still in the ignition, and the best parking spot on the moon is officially reserved.

novo6.full_text: Imagine a robot no bigger than your school backpack, weighing just 23 pounds. Back in 1997, critics laughed. They said a rover on Mars was pure fantasy. They said it would get stuck on the first pebble, freeze in the first night, or flip upside down. On the 4th of July, 1997, our mothership bounced across an ancient dried up Martian riverbed inside 20 giant airbags. When the petals unfolded, our six little aluminum wheels rolled down the ramps into the red sand. We were named Sojourner, in honor of Sojourner Truth, the great fighter for human freedom. We were built to last seven days. We survived for 83. We tundled up to giant boulders named Barnacle Bill and Yogi, pressed our tiny sensor against them, and proved that Mars was once washed by catastrophic torrents of liquid water. When the winter cold finally drained our circuits, we came to rest in Aries, Valus. Every giant rover roaming Mars today, spirit, opportunity, curiosity, perseverance, walks in the tiny tire tracks we left behind. Big dreams start small.

novo7.full_text: Travel with your mind, beyond the moon, beyond Mars, beyond the orbits of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Out where the sun is just another sparkling diamond in the black sea of space, travels pioneer 10. Launched in 1972, we were the first machine built by human hands to sail into the unknown. Scientists didn't even know if a spacecraft could pass through the asteroid belt without being crushed into dust. We sailed straight through without a scratch. We braved the crushing radiation belts of Jupiter to send back humanity's first breathtaking close-ups of the great red spot, and bolted to our antenna star, and the address of Earth written in the rhythm of pulsing stars. In 2003, our radio grew two weeks to reach home. But our journey did not end. We are coasting toward the star Aldebaran in the constellation Taurus. It will take us two million years to arrive. Long after our creators have returned to stardust, we will still be carrying humanity's postcard through the Milky Way. Proof that on a small blue planet, there lived creatures who dared to touch the stars.

novo8.full_text: In 1967, the greatest scientists in the world were paralyzed by fear. They warned that the moon's surface might be a bottomless pit of pulverized cosmic dust and that any astronaut who stepped out of a spaceship would sink, suffocate, and vanish. We were sent into the dark to touch down and find out. We bounced three times in a crater in the ocean of storms, planted our three foot pads, and extended a little mechanical arm. We dug into the lunar dirt and proved the ground was as firm as damp beach sand. We signaled earth. The ground will hold you. Come on up. And then, two and a half years later, the impossible happened. A thunderous roar shook the dust. Apollo 12 landed just 500 feet away. Two astronauts, Pete Conrad and Alan Bean, walked right across the lunar crater, walked right up to our foot pads, and greeted us! They unbolted our television camera and brought it home to earth to study how deep space weathers materials. We are the only robot in history to be visited by human travelers on an alien world. We were the scout who stayed behind, and our friends came to visit.
